Reject. The proposed plan—deleting the existing storage before the replacement is restored—puts every byte of data you currently hold at risk of permanent, unrecoverable loss, and the ordering of operations is the single most important decision in any storage cutover. The fundamental problem is that the plan inverts the safety principle that should govern all migration work: you must never destroy the source before you have verified that the destination is complete, consistent, and accessible. By deleting first, you are betting the entire operation on the assumption that the replacement will restore without error, without partial failure, without a corrupted snapshot, without a network interruption mid-transfer, and without a configuration mismatch that only surfaces after the old data is already gone. In practice, none of those assumptions are safe to make, and the cost of being wrong is not a retry or a rollback—it is the total loss of data that may exist in no other copy.

Consider what can go wrong between the moment you issue the delete command and the moment the replacement storage is fully restored and verified. The restore process itself can fail partway through. A disk in the target array can die during the write. A network link carrying the backup stream can drop. The backup file you are restoring from can be silently corrupted, a problem that only becomes apparent when you try to open a file or run a checksum. The replacement hardware or virtual volume can present a different block size, a different filesystem layout, or a different permission model that makes the restored data technically present but functionally unusable. Any one of these failures, occurring after the old storage is already deleted, leaves you with no fallback. You cannot "just put the old storage back." You cannot roll the delete command forward in time. The data is gone, and the only remaining path is to attempt a restore from a backup that may be days or weeks old, meaning you lose every transaction,
